extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate and beginning researchers (students) and anyone planning an academic research project
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing a research topic, narrowing it, formulating answerable questions, identifying and finding appropriate data, and motivating the question's significance for readers. Emphasizes iterative writing, group feedback, and distinguishing practical vs. conceptual research problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the kind of evidence readers expect
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the kind of evidence your readers will expect you to offer in support of your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether readers will accept reports of facts from secondary sources or will expect you to consult primary sources; whether they expect quantitative data, quotations from authorities, or firsthand observations. Tailor your research strategy to the evidentiary expectations of your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm you can find the necessary data before starting
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether you can find those data. There's no point starting research on a topic until you know you have a good chance of finding data on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your library or resources lack relevant sources, reconsider the topic. For advanced projects, check special collections or institutional strengths before committing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptualize 'data' broadly and convert it to evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: By data we mean not just numbers but anything you find 'out there' relevant to answering your research question — quotations, historical facts, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data are inert until used to support a claim; once used to support a claim they become evidence. If you don't have data you can use as evidence, you haven't collected enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write regularly and use writing-to-discover
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to do lots of writing along the way; much of it will be routine note-taking, but you should also write reflectively to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make outlines; explain why you disagree with a source; draw diagrams to connect disparate facts; summarize sources and record random thoughts. Keep a journal for hunches and problems. This process improves critical thinking and makes drafting more productive, even if much won't appear in the final draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and use a writing group
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a writing partner or a small group to discuss progress, review drafts, and provide discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meet regularly; early meetings should start with a three-part sentence: 'I'm working on X because I want to find out Y, so that I (and you) can better understand Z.' Develop an 'elevator story' summarizing research question, best-guess answer, and expected evidence. Discuss readers and whether they will trust the evidence. Check instructor rules about collaboration for class assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start topic selection from personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can work on any topic, start with what most interests you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List many interests without filtering for what you think will impress a teacher. Commitment to the topic contributes more to quality than initial sophistication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bibliographies, encyclopedias, and controlled searches to find topic angles
rubrics_metrics.description: In the library, look up your topic in general bibliographies and specialized guides; on the Internet, use web encyclopedias and the references they cite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Readers' Guide, American Humanities Index, Encyclopaedia Britannica, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, and specialized indexes. On the Web, prefer sources similar to library materials; copy reference lists from encyclopedias; use Wikipedia for ideas but always confirm in reliable sources and never cite Wikipedia (unless studying Wikipedia itself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use scholarly search tools for focused topics
rubrics_metrics.description: For more focused or advanced projects, use specialized indexes and Google Scholar to find how others have narrowed similar topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skim headings in Philosopher's Index, Psychological Abstracts, Women's Studies Abstracts; skim recent journal issues, conference programs, calls for papers, and library new arrivals to identify current debates and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow overly broad topics using action/relationship words
rubrics_metrics.description: A topic is too broad if you can state it in four or five words; narrow it by adding nouns derived from verbs expressing actions or relationships (e.g., conflict, contribution, development).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert static topics into sentences that imply action or relationship so they become claims worth supporting. Example transformations show how adding conflict/description/developing turns a vague topic into a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrowing a topic so much that data are unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't narrow your topic so much that you can't find data on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance specificity with availability of sources. Example: too-specific technical design decisions on an early prototype may lack sufficient accessible data for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulate specific questions before plowing through sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't immediately start plowing through all the sources and taking notes; instead formulate questions that point you to just the data you need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting data for their own sake produces pastiche; specific questions let you select relevant data and build an answer worth supporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize how and why questions over who/what/when/where
rubrics_metrics.description: You can start with journalistic questions, but focus on how and why to invite deeper thinking and more interesting answers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To engage critical thinking, systematically ask about history, composition, categories, and other dimensions (see subsequent sub-criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask about the history of your topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how the topic fits into a larger developmental context, its internal history, and how it changed through time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Why did masks come into being? How have Halloween masks or Native American masks changed? How has the role of masks in society changed?

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask about structure and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how the topic fits into a larger structure or system and how its parts fit together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: How do masks reflect societal values? What parts of a mask are significant in a ceremony, and why? Consider colors, coverage, and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask about categorization and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask how your topic can be grouped into kinds and how it compares with similar topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Different kinds of masks by appearance/use/geography; how Native American ceremonial masks differ from Japanese masks; comparison with Mardi Gras or Halloween masks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turn positive questions into negative ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Recast questions to ask why something has not occurred or what is not the case to open new perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Why have masks not become part of other holidays? What parts of masks are typically not significant?

rubrics_metrics.name: Use speculative 'what if' questions to explore consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask counterfactual or speculative questions to imagine different contexts and their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: What if no one wore masks except for safety? What if everyone wore masks in public? Use such thought experiments to surface new areas of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask questions suggested by your sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Let sources suggest questions that extend claims, test them with new evidence, or apply analogous questions to related topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for open questions in journal articles, online discussion lists, and use disagreements with sources to devise further research questions. Only post questions to lists if appropriate for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate candidate questions for research-worthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate questions to ensure they invite new thinking: avoid settled-fact questions, wholly speculative questions without data, and dead-end trivia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer questions whose answers could change understanding of a larger issue. Note exceptions: seemingly trivial questions can sometimes yield important discoveries (example: coffee-ring fluid dynamics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine related questions into larger, significant questions
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have several promising questions, combine them into a single more significant question that captures broader interests and implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Combine questions about motives and effects of storytellers into 'How and why have users of the Alamo story given the event a mythic quality?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the question's significance using a three-part sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain: (1) what you are writing about, (2) what you don't know about it, and (3) why readers should care — using the three-step formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 1: Name your topic ('I am studying...'). Step 2: Add an indirect question ('because I want to find out how/why/whether...'). Step 3: Motivate with 'in order to help my reader understand...' giving the 'So what?' that shows the reader why the question matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularly test and communicate the three-step framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask others (roommate, relative, friend) to force you to flesh out the three-step sentence so you know where you are and what you must still do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if you cannot fully articulate all steps early, practicing this framing clarifies progress and helps ensure the work will be valued by your research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish practical problems from academic research problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the difference between practical problems (What should we do?) and conceptual academic problems (What should we think?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical problems are caused by conditions that require action; research problems arise from lack of understanding and are solved by answering questions that improve understanding. Solving practical problems often requires first solving a research problem that defines what is not understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use research problems to motivate practical solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that practical solutions usually follow from solving a research problem that clarifies causes and options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphical relationship: practical problem motivates research; research answers define the practical solution. Examples include diagnosing plant cost increases or identifying brake repair options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure a topic will interest others, not just you
rubrics_metrics.description: Work toward articulating why others in your field should care about your question — the 'So what?' — to enter the conversation of your research community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advanced researchers sometimes begin with questions already of interest to the community. If you cannot fully answer why it matters early on, continue developing the three-step framing as your project progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use library and field-specific resource checks when choosing topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Before settling on a topic, make sure your library or nearby institutions have at least some relevant sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not, you may need to choose another topic or seek alternate libraries/resources; advanced projects can exploit unique local collections as an entry point.
